# Incentives for teachers: A theoretical framework and a structural model

Ronak Jain†

Nuﬃeld College

Supervisors: Margaret Meyer and Ian Crawford

Submitted in partial fulﬁlment of the requirements for the degree of the Master of Philosophy in Economics

## Abstract

This study provides structural analysis of teacher behaviour under the provision of individual and group monetary incentive schemes using data from a randomised control trial conducted in India (Muralidharan and Sundaraman, 2011). I develop a theoretical principal-agent model explicitly allowing for both intrinsic motivation and a crowding out eﬀect of explicit performance pay on intrinsic incentives. Theoretically, I show that intrinsic motivation and extrinsic motivation through performance pay are substitutes under the optimal incentive scheme in the presence of motivation crowding out. Applying the theoretical framework for structural analysis, I identify the sets of teacher heterogeneity consistent with each eﬀort choice in the treatment and control group schools. Using the barycenters of these sets, I calculate that increasing the eﬀort of the average teacher who did not change his/her eﬀort under the experimental incentive payment of Rs. 500, would require increasing the incentive bonus to Rs. 730 under the individual incentive scheme. The corresponding ﬁgure lies between Rs. 720 - Rs. 1020 depending on the reported group cooperation level under the group incentive scheme.

Keywords: performance pay, structural model, group incentives, intrinsic motivation, motivation crowding out, set identiﬁcation

## 1 Introduction

Given the importance of the role of a teacher in a child’s education, it is important to have an understanding of how incentives might aﬀect a teacher’s motivation level and student learning outcomes. Indeed, the signiﬁcance of this is even greater for developing economies where teacher absenteeism and low teacher eﬀort is a matter of concern. The ﬁndings of a disconcertingly high absenteeism rate of 25% in Indian government primary schools (Kremer et al., 2005) and a similar ﬁnding for a number of other developing economies (Chaudhury et al., 2006, EFA Global Monitoring Report, 2014) calls for the need to explore how incentives can be employed to redress the situation.

To answer this question one might naturally turn to the theoretical literature on the subject for predictions regarding the eﬀectiveness of using incentives for workers more broadly. Theoretically, however, there are no unequivocal predictions regarding the eﬀectiveness of using incentives for teachers. Prima facie, whilst the canonical economic theory of incentives suggests that an agent will exert higher eﬀort when incentivised with a higher marginal return for a task (Sappington, 1991), given that a teacher’s role is likely to require multi-tasking – with responsibilities requiring, inter alia, marking students’ work, monitoring students’ progress, building students’ non-cognitive skills, exam preparation and teaching – it is diﬃcult to predict with certainty the consequences of incentive provision (Holmstrom and Milgrom, 1991).

Moreover, the inability to measure a teacher’s eﬀort directly makes it necessary to condition the incentive provision on a more easily quantiﬁable performance measure that is indicative of the eﬀort exerted (Baker, 1992, Baker, 2000, Neal, 2011). Furthermore, if teachers are public servants, they are likely to diﬀer systematically from those who teach in the private sector, for example, in terms of their motivation level or image concerns (Besley and Ghatak, 2005 & 2008). Hence, the eﬀect of incentive provision for teachers is likely to be contingent on a number of factors.

In light of these theoretical contingencies of the eﬀects of incentive provision, there is a growing interest amongst researchers to use experiments to evaluate the eﬀectiveness of using incentives empirically. A number of studies have highlighted that the the potential unintended consequences of incentive provision, such as crowding out of intrinsic motivation or signalling distrust on the part of the principal, can make incentive provision counter productive in diﬀerent contexts (Frey and Oberholzer-Gee, 1997, Gneezy and Rustichini,

2000, Falk and Kosfeld, 2006, Ariely et al., 2009, Fuster and Meier, 2010, Gneezy et al., 2011). The magnitude of the incentive and how the agent perceives a particular form of incentive also is noted to play an important role in avoiding perverse outcomes (Gneezy and Rustichini, 2000). Focusing in particular on incentives in education, Neal (2011) provides an excellent and concise overview of the mixed outcomes of some of the experiments conducted in the last two decades. The ﬁndings of these studies further attest to the diﬃculty of predicting the eﬀects of an incentive program ex-ante and serve to highlight some of the nuances that the design of an incentive program should take into consideration.

In this line of enquiry, cognizant of the importance of the context in determining the eﬀects of incentive provision, there have been a number of recent experimental studies involving teachers in developing economies. Evaluating the usefulness of monitoring combined with ﬁnancial incentives for teachers in rural India, an experimental study by Duﬂo et al.(2012) found that providing incentives was eﬀective in reducing teacher absenteeism by 21 percentage points and increased student test scores by 0.17 standard deviation. The results of another experimental study in India by Muralidharan and Sundararaman (2011) also point to a signiﬁcant and positive eﬀect - an increase in student math and language scores by 0.27 and 0.17 standard deviations respectively - of performance related pay. Interestingly, this study also found positive spillovers on non-incentivised subjects.

However, a recent experimental study by Barrera-Osorio and Raju (2017) involving bonuses to teachers in Pakistan found no improvement in test scores though enrolment and exam participation of students increased. Similarly, whilst the results of Glewwe et al.(2010) involving Kenyan primary school teachers suggest a positive impact of performance linked pay on incentivised subjects, there was no improvement in teacher attendance or positive spillovers to other non-incentivised subjects. Taken as a whole, results from these experimental studies in developing countries are suggestive of a positive eﬀect of incentivising teachers, although they diﬀer on the precise outcome inﬂuenced and the extent to which it was aﬀected.

Importantly, although experimental studies can help to judge the end result of providing incentives, an understanding of the precise mechanism through which the eﬀect is brought about is left wanting by relying solely on this method to approach the question. Still nascent but a promising approach in the ﬁeld is to use experimental studies in conjunction with a structural model to better understand the underlying mechanism driving the end-line

Philosopher Immanuel Kant reasoned that “concepts without percepts are empty, percepts without concepts are blind”, arguing that concepts, such as space and time, are a prerequisite for us to have intelligible perceptual experience.2 Analogously, I believe that a theoretical model enables us to interpret the mechanisms driving the reduced form results obtained from empirical studies and empirical analysis acts as a check for predictions of the theoretical model. Structural modelling, incorporating both theoretical and empirical analysis, therefore is an invaluable tool to use in this context to better understand the eﬀects of providing incentives to teachers. Structural analysis also oﬀers the possibility to conduct counter factual policy analysis by varying the experiment’s parameters, which in the case of an experimental incentive program, oﬀers an economical way to arrive at an optimal incentive formula.3 It is in this respect that this study seeks to make a contribution to the existing literature in the ﬁeld.

This study ﬁrst outlines a simple theoretical framework which can be used to analyse performance related pay for teachers based on improvement in student test scores. It then uses the framework to explain the ﬁndings of the randomised control trial in India which provided ﬁnancial incentives of Rs. 500 to government primary school teachers based on improvement in student achievement (Muralidharan and Sundararaman, 2011). Subsequently, based on this theoretical framework, I estimate a structural model using the data from this experiment to investigate teacher behaviour with explicit monetary incentives. Given the very optimistic results of the experiment brieﬂy outlined earlier, I believe it is a worthwhile exercise to explore the underlying choice behaviour to be more conﬁdent in our understanding of how incentives can be used to motivate teachers in India and in other developing countries.

This experimental study was conducted in schools in Andhra Pradesh, India.4

The experiment had one treatment group of schools where teachers received bonuses based on the performance of their students (teacher-level incentives) and another group of schools where teachers received bonus pay based on

Motivation for the study

Going further than the existing literature on the subject, I address the lacuna in the theoretical literature on the interaction of explicit monetary incentives and intrinsic motivation. To this end, I develop a theoretical principal-agent model incorporating both intrinsic motivation and a crowding-out eﬀect of explicit performance pay on intrinsic incentives.

Theoretically, I ﬁnd that under the individual incentive scheme, the optimal incentive pay is decreasing in a teacher’s intrinsic motivation and the extent to which a teacher experiences motivation crowding out. When providing group-level incentives, I ﬁnd that the optimal incentive pay is decreasing in a teacher’s intrinsic motivation and if the teachers are similar in terms of their ability and the extent to which they experience motivation crowding out, then the optimal incentive pay is also decreasing in their motivation crowding out. Hence, when providing individual-level or group incentives, extrinsic and intrinsic motivation act as substitutes for the principal under the optimal incentive contract. Interestingly, for a given incentive payment schedule, if a teacher experiences high motivation crowding out but is also highly altruistic towards other teacher’s earnings from the incentive scheme, then providing group-level incentives could dominate individual-level incentives for incentivising eﬀort.

Using structural analysis for the experiment, refraining from making any untestable parametric assumptions about the nature of the underlying teacher heterogeneity or treating it simply as a multivariate error term, I instead use a set identiﬁcation strategy for empirical analysis. I ﬁnd that the density of intrinsic motivation in the control schools is bimodal with teachers either hav-

ing very low or medium levels of intrinsic motivation. I also identify the set for teacher heterogeneity consistent with each eﬀort choice in the treatment schools. Using these sets, I then derive the bounds for the incentive payment needed to raise teachers’ eﬀorts. I ﬁnd that the upper bound for the increase in incentive payment needed depends on the underlying teacher heterogeneity; in particular, it is decreasing in the teachers’ ability and increasing in teachers’ motivation crowding out. I also show that it is comparatively less costly to incentivise all teachers to increase their eﬀort by one if their initial eﬀort choice was unchanged under the experiment than if the teachers did increase their eﬀort under the experimental scheme. Furthermore, I ﬁnd that the cost of increasing all teachers’ eﬀorts from that chosen under the experiment is increasing in the magnitude of the increase in eﬀort required.

More concretely, I ﬁnd that increasing the eﬀort of the average teacher who did not change his/her eﬀort under the incentive scheme, would require increasing the incentive bonus to Rs. 730 for the individual-level incentives whilst the ﬁgure lies between Rs. 720 - Rs. 1020 depending on the reported group cooperation level among teachers when providing group incentives. For increasing the change in eﬀort of the teachers not choosing the maximal level of eﬀort under the original payment scheme, we would need an incentive payment of at least Rs. 1020 under individual-level incentives and at-least Rs. 850 - Rs. 1020 under the group incentive payment scheme depending on the reported group cooperation level among teachers.

## 2 A brief overview of the experiment

The experiment gave primary school teachers incentives based on either their own students’ test performance (individual-level incentives) or the test performance of all the students in their school (group incentives). The randomised control trial involved 300 government-run primary schools in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh over the time period 2005-07.5 100 schools

## 3 Theoretical Framework

### 3.1 Provision of individual-level incentives with intrinsically motivated agents

Individuals vary considerably in their level of intrinsic motivation. A number of studies have noted the importance of intrinsic motivation in inﬂuencing the behaviour of workers and have highlighted the possible danger of monetary incentives displacing this.7 In light of these studies, I model teachers as motivated agents and going beyond the existing theoretical literature on incentives, I explicitly allow for the possibility of a motivation crowding out eﬀect in the utility function.

In order to focus on illustrating how the eﬀectiveness of providing incentives varies with the level of one’s intrinsic motivation, I use a stylised static model. Rather than restricting the analysis strictly to the experimental setting, the theoretical framework outlined here examines the use of performance related pay based on student improvement more broadly. ### 4.2 Set Identiﬁcation of Teacher Heterogeneity

I now turn to identify the structural parameters in the theoretical model using this data. Diﬀerent sets of structural parameters are identiﬁable for the control and treatment groups given the assumptions about what factors aﬀect the choices made by the teachers in each scenario.51 As the eﬀort choice in this setting is observed as a discrete rather than a continuous variable, instead of using the incentive compatibility constraint which derives the eﬀort choice of the teacher assuming continuity of eﬀort, I work directly with the utility function for structural estimation.52

I depart from the standard approach of treating unobserved heterogeneity as a multivariate error term as is often motivated in a random utility framework; instead I use a set identiﬁcation strategy for the following reasons. If we denote θi as the vector of heterogeneous parameters and xij as the observable characteristics driving the eﬀort choice j of the teacher i, we can write the utility function of the teacher as speciﬁed in the theoretical section as U(θi, xij). It is therefore important to note ﬁrstly that the theoretical framework does not specify any additional structure such as the joint distribution of θi. Standard estimation techniques, such as Maximum (Simulated) Likelihood, rely on parametric distributional assumptions regarding the joint or marginal distribution of the unobservable heterogeneity and therefore necessitate additional untestable assumptions regarding the nature of underlying

### 5.2 Extensions

This study has outlined a simple static framework for analysing the optimal incentive pay for teachers based on improvement in student test scores. While this framework is suﬃcient to analyse the interaction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and to illustrate the tradeoﬀthat the principal may face between incentives and motivation crowding out, extending the model to allow for dynamic contracting is an important next step. This can help us analyse how the optimal incentive intensity may evolve as the teachers’ reference points for eﬀort change and how extrinsic and intrinsic motivation may interact in the presence of dynamic incentives. Nonetheless, the results derived from the framework used here will continue to hold for teachers who have a very low discount factor and/or assigned a low probability for the continuation of the program for the second year.

Another potential for extension is to allow for psychic costs of eﬀort that can vary between teachers. This would allow the unobservable teacher heterogeneity to be four-dimensional. However, while allowing the model to be more ﬂexible, this would make it considerably less tractable without adding signiﬁcantly to the insights gained thus far.61

The analysis here leaves room for taking a further step back and investigating the optimality of performance pay design formally - whether incentives should be given at the individual level or at the group level. An interesting direction for building on this framework is to analyse and compare individual and group level performance pay in a dynamic setting. Further, an exciting open research question is to investigate teacher behaviour under non-monetary incentives, comparing its cost eﬀectiveness to that of monetary incentives.

Finally, as the focus of this study has been to analyse teacher eﬀort under incentive provision taking a simple student test score and human capital technology, there is scope for varying the functional forms of these production functions in order to analyse what level of eﬀort is optimal to incentivise under each case. The analysis here has provided a simple and tractable characterisation of what the teachers may believe the technology of test scores to be and the results will continue to hold if the teachers are uncertain of the precise technology.

## 6 Conclusion

This study has outlined a simple theoretical framework which can be used to analyse performance related pay for teachers based on improvement in student test scores. Building on and going beyond the existing work in this ﬁeld, I address the lacuna in the theoretical literature on the interaction of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation through explicit performance related pay. In light of the psychological and experimental literature on possible perverse and unintended consequences of explicit monetary rewards, I model teachers as motivated agents and allow for a motivation crowding out eﬀect. The model highlights how the dimensions of heterogeneity among teachers - their ability, intrinsic motivation, extent to which they experience motivation crowding out due to explicit performance pay and internalisation of the externality of their eﬀort on the other team members’ earnings - and their interactions are important in determining teacher eﬀort under incentives.

Using a principal-agent framework, I ﬁnd that the optimal incentive pay is decreasing in a teacher’s intrinsic motivation and the extent to which a teacher experiences motivation crowding out under the individual incentive scheme. Under the group incentive scheme, I ﬁnd that the optimal incentive pay is decreasing in a teacher’s intrinsic motivation, and if the teachers are similar in terms of their ability and the extent to which they experience motivation crowding out, then the optimal incentive pay is also decreasing in their motivation crowding out. Therefore, under the optimal incentive contract extrinsic and intrinsic motivation act as substitutes for the principal both under the individual and group incentive scheme. An interesting implication of the model is that for a given incentive payment scheme, if a teacher experiences high motivation crowding out and is also highly altruistic towards other teacher’s earnings from the incentive scheme, then group incentive scheme could be better than individual incentive scheme if the objective is to increase teacher eﬀort.

I then show how this framework can be used to explain and analyse the ﬁndings of the randomised control trial in India conducted by Muralidharan and Sundararaman (2011). Answering the questions I set out to investigate, I ﬁnd that the teachers in the treatment schools on average increase their eﬀort by more relative to the control group schools. This is in line with the theoretical prediction of the model and suggests that teachers do not experience 100% motivation crowding out and may place some weight on the other teachers’ earnings when given group incentives. Subsequently, using

57


<!-- Page 58 -->


this theoretical framework, I estimate a structural model using the data from this experiment to further investigate teacher behaviour.

In structural analysis, I refrain from making any untestable assumptions about the underlying distribution of unobservable heterogeneity or simply treating it as a multivariate error term. Instead, I bound the set of heterogeneous parameters using the necessary conditions that the set must satisfy if the choice behaviour were generated by the theoretical model, thereby adopting a set identiﬁcation strategy. I estimate the density of intrinsic motivation in the control group schools and ﬁnd that is bimodal with most teachers either having very low or medium levels of intrinsic motivation. For treatment group schools, I identify the set for teacher heterogeneity consistent with each eﬀort choice. Using these sets, I then obtain the bounds for the incentive payment needed to raise teachers’ eﬀorts and I ﬁnd that the upper bound for the increase in incentive payment needed varies with the underlying teacher heterogeneity predictably. In particular, it is decreasing in the teachers’ ability and increasing in teachers’ motivation crowding out. I also illustrate that it is comparatively less costly to incentivise all teachers to increase their eﬀort by one if their initial eﬀort choice was unchanged under the experiment than if the teachers did increase their eﬀort under the experimental scheme. Furthermore, I ﬁnd that the cost of increasing all teachers’ eﬀorts from that chosen under the experiment is increasing in the magnitude of the increase in eﬀort required.

Using structural assumptions and deriving the barycenters of the identiﬁed sets of teacher heterogeneity, I ﬁnd that increasing the eﬀort of the average teacher who did not change his/her eﬀort under the individual incentive scheme, would need a higher bonus payment of Rs. 730. The same ﬁgure lies between Rs. 720 - Rs. 1020, depending on the reported group cooperation level among teachers, when providing group incentives. Furthermore, I estimate that increasing the change in eﬀort of the teachers not choosing the maximal level of eﬀort under the original payment scheme, would require an incentive payment of at least Rs. 1020 under individual-level incentives and at least Rs. 850 - Rs. 1020 under the group incentive payment scheme depending on the reported group cooperation level among the teachers.

I have argued that this simple static framework is suﬃcient to analyse the interaction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and to shed light on the tradeoﬀthat the principal may face between incentive provision and motivation crowding out. It goes without saying, however, that extending the model to allow for dynamic contracting is an important next step and may

Investigating how the optimal incentive intensity evolves as the teachers’ reference points for eﬀort change and how extrinsic and intrinsic motivation interact in the presence of dynamic incentives is an exciting research endeavour. The results derived from the model used here will nonetheless continue to hold for teachers who have a very low discount factor and/or assigned a low probability for the continuation of the program for the second year. Some interesting avenues and extensions of the analysis here would be to allow for psychic costs of eﬀort as another dimension of heterogeneity, to compare teacher behaviour under non-monetary incentives and to vary the student test score technology to investigate the optimal eﬀort level to incentivise under diﬀerent scenarios.
